New office development in Apac becoming more selective; Singapore among markets facing constraints
article:
New development in the Asia Pacific (Apac) office market is becoming more selective as higher construction costs, elevated borrowing costs and lack of new supply challenge viability, according to Cushman & Wakefield.

In a November research report titled Global Office Supply: The Development Drought, the firm highlights a global slowdown in office development activity.

It estimates around 580 million sq ft of office space under construction globally in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 45% shortfall compared to the 3Q2017 peak of 1.04 billion sq ft. This puts global office development at its lowest level in a decade.

Cushman & Wakefield attribute the drop in new office construction to “higher for longer” interest rates and soaring construction costs stemming from trade disruptions related to the Suez Canal blockage and geopolitical tensions.

In its report, Cushman & Wakefield examined the viability of office markets across the globe by measuring economic rent: the minimum rent a new office development needs to earn to be profitable, after factoring land acquisition and development costs, operational costs, the developer’s margin, and borrowing costs.

“Comparing economic rent with prime market rent shows how close a market is to viability, and therefore to unlocking new supply,” the firm explains. Market rent on par or exceeding economic rent indicates an office market viable for new developments.

In Apac, the average economic rent is currently about 1% below prime market rents. By 2030, Cushman & Wakefield expect economic rent to exceed market rent by about 7%, implying limited viability for future developments across the region.

However, beyond the headline figures, viability diverges between individual markets, notes Dr Dominic Brown, head of international research and Global Think Tank at Cushman & Wakefield.

Major office markets in Apac, including Singapore, Tokyo and Sydney are seeing viability becoming more constrained as development economics “come under increasing pressure”, says Brown.

In contrast, Seoul and Bengaluru have emerged as standout markets for new supply, supported by strong occupier demand and rental growth.

In Singapore, prime market rents have largely tracked economic rents since 2023, according to the report. The trend is expected to continue until 2028, after which new Grade A supply from developments such as The Clifford, The Skywaters and One Comcentre , will test market absorption for backfill space.

While development opportunities "remain viable" in Singapore in the near term, Cushman & Wakefield expects future Grade A supply to be driven by redevelopment of older stock rather than fresh projects.

For Tokyo, prime market rents are currently 22% above economic rents, supported by tight vacancy. However, this margin is expected to be eroded in the coming years by rising financing costs and capitalisation rates, resulting in viability turning negative from 2030 onwards.

Sydney has the largest feasibility gap in Apac, which market rents currently 24% below economic rents. In addition to labour shortages and higher material and freight costs, pipelines for housing, infrastructure and and data centre developments are crowding out commercial projects, adding hurdles for new office development, say Cushman & Wakefield.

On the flipside, Seoul’s office market is expected to stay viable, thanks to steady demand underpinned by growing AI-related investment and strong semiconductor exports. In 2026, prime office rent in the South Korean capital stood 26% more than economic rent, with 20.7 million sq ft of office space currently under construction.

While the gap between market rent and economic rent is expected to narrow to 6% by 2030 and 5% and 2035 due to rising capitalisation rates, resilient demand is expected to keep the office market viable for new projects.

Similarly, new office developments in India’s Bengaluru are expected to be feasible through to 2035. Prime market rents, which currently sit at 16% above economic rents, are expected to grow 5% annually, outpacing economic rent growth of 2.5% per year.

Amid the divergent Apac office landscape, occupiers will have to tailor real estate strategies according to the market, says Anshul Jain, head of Apac offices and retail at Cushman & Wakefield.

“Organisations that actively review their portfolio strategies and have a clear view of local market dynamics will be better positioned to manage costs and secure quality space that support their long-term office needs,” he says.

title: Is the Great Singapore REIT Comeback Finally Here?
article:
Singapore
real estate investment trusts
(REITs) have had a frustrating couple of years.
The
iEdge S-REIT Index
(SGX: SRU) was down about 14.1% year to date as at 13 November 2026 against the
Straits Times Index’s
(SGX: ^STI) 12.3% gain.
Yet, some REITs are quietly growing their distributions again.
So, is this the start of a proper recovery or just a pause before the next leg down?
The answer depends on more than interest rates.
Why Singapore REITs Have Struggled and What’s Different Now
Higher interest rates
did most of the damage.
When rates went up, REITs had to refinance their loans at higher costs, leaving less to pay out as distributions per unit (DPU).
Meanwhile, income investors could earn a decent return from T-bills and fixed deposits without taking any risk.
Some REITs also struggled with falling property values or weak overseas performance, while banks and growth stocks pulled money away.
Some of that pressure is lifting.
Local interest rates have eased, so older loans are being refinanced more cheaply.
Singapore offices and malls are signing leases at higher rents, occupancy rates are still firm, and many REITs still trade below their net asset value (NAV).
If these trends hold, the three REITs below could benefit.

Suntec looks the most defensive, NTT DC REIT has the clearest growth, and SET offers the highest yield for those willing to take on more risk.
Suntec REIT (SGX: T82U) – Strong Rents That Benefit From Lower Rates
Suntec REIT is best known for Suntec City, and it also owns stakes in One Raffles Quay and Marina Bay Financial Centre.
Outside Singapore, it has offices in Australia and the UK.
Business at home is going well.
As at 30 September 2026 (3Q2026), its Singapore offices were 99.6% occupied and its malls 98.6%.
In 3Q2026, rental reversions were 7.3% for its Singapore offices and 11.2% for its malls.
DPU for the first nine months (9M2026) rose 20.7% year on year (YoY), helped by lower interest costs.
At a unit price of S$1.35 as at 13 November 2026, Suntec REIT offers a trailing distribution yield of 6.0% and trades at about 0.66x its net asset value (NAV) of S$2.04 per unit.
The main weakness is debt.
Gearing climbed to 43.0%, and an interest coverage ratio (ICR) of 2.3x.
Its all-in financing cost has fallen to 3.57%, from 3.71% at 31 December 2025.
Should Suntec manage to sell its three Australian assets, gearing could improve from current levels.
Management expects future DPU growth to be from higher Singapore rents and lower financing costs.
The main risks for Suntec would likely be from its overseas holdings and higher financing costs.
NTT DC REIT (SGX: NTDU) – The Growth Recovery Play
This data centre REIT owns six properties in the US, Austria, and Singapore.
That’s a rare corner of property where rents are still climbing at a healthy clip.
Its maiden DPU, ending 31 March 2026 (FY2025/2026), came in at US$0.0556.
At a unit price of US$0.945 as at 13 November 2026, this works out to an estimated distribution yield of 5.9%.
Do note this distribution covered less than a full year.
For the first quarter ended 30 June 2026 (1QFY2026/2027), portfolio occupancy was 95.9% (rising to 99.2% once signed leases start), and renewals were signed at rents 13.4% higher.
The balance sheet leaves plenty of room for acquisition-fuelled growth.
Gearing is at 31%, while its ICR stands at 4.7x.
No loans fall due for two years, and the REIT has US$261 million of debt headroom before it reaches its 40% gearing limit.
The main risks include rising power costs, 14% of rent that’s up for renewal in this financial year, and a concentrated tenant base where the top 10 pay 74.5% of rent.
Stoneweg Europe Stapled Trust (SGX: SET) – The High-Yield Opportunity
Stoneweg Europe, or SET, owns mostly logistics and office properties across Europe.
At a unit price of €1.50 as at 13 November 2026, it yields about 9.0% and trades at roughly 0.74x NAV.
The distribution looks steady for now.
Distribution per stapled security (DPS) rose 1.4% to €0.0664 in 1H2026 (ended 30 June 2026), and management expects the full-year figure to be broadly in line with FY2025.
Logistics rental reversion was 9.6%, with a healthy occupancy rate of 95.2%, so why are the units trading near 52-week lows?
Offices are the drag.
Occupancy is only at 90.3%, and office rental reversion was down 4.1%.
Gearing looks manageable at 41.9%, with an ICR of 3.0x.
Crucially, 90% of its debt is hedged, and there’s no major refinancing until 2030.
This gives the REIT some time before its office segment recovers.
SET is also moving into data centres, which could provide some potential upside, but this brings execution risk.
On balance, the yield is tempting, but you’re being paid to accept weaker office performance and a big strategy shift (into data centres).
What Could Stop the REIT Comeback?
Another Fed rate hike, or rates that stay elevated, would keep refinancing costs up.
Weaker rents, further declines in property values or fresh DPU cuts would also hurt.
Finally, the continued preference for
banks
, risk-free income alternatives, or growth stocks could keep investors away from REITs.
Cheap REITs can stay cheap if the reasons behind the discount don’t change.
Get Smart: A Recovery Worth Watching
S-REITs could be close to a turning point, though a lot still depends on where interest rates go.
And even if sentiment picks up, some REITs will recover much faster than others.
The ones to look for have growing rents and debt that’s under control, because those are the REITs most able to raise DPU.
Investors who focus on these qualities may be well placed if the sector’s recovery takes hold.

title: Vujcic says bets on ECB hike in 2027 don’t seem unreasonable
article:
(Nov 16): Market wagers on the European Central Bank (ECB) tightening monetary policy in 2027 may prove accurate, Vice President Boris Vujcic said, becoming one of the first officials to discuss moves beyond an expected hike next month.

Reiterating that there’s no pre-determined path for borrowing costs, the Croatian official said the current inflation outlook warrants a continued measured response, suggesting interest rates will rise further following two increases since the Iran war began.

“Pricing of another rate hike next year does not seem unreasonable from where we stand at the moment,” Vujcic said on Monday in Frankfurt. “But there’s much to happen between now and then.”

Inflation is currently running at twice the ECB’s 2% target, while the economy is holding up well in the face of multiple headwinds. Investors are currently betting on two quarter-point increases in the deposit rate in 2027, following one in December. Most analysts surveyed by Bloomberg, however, don’t see the ECB moving beyond next month.

Vujcic’s comments echo Lithuanian central bank governor Gediminas Simkus, who told Econostream Media that rates may have to be lifted further in 2027.

See also: Thai GDP growth rebounds as AI drives investments, exports

“I’m not sure that December’s hike alone would be enough,” the Lithuanian official said in an interview published on Monday. “Further tightening next year might be necessary, depending on the inflation outlook and strength of policy transmission.”

title: Korea’s instant ramen giants take their spicy rivalry global
article:
(Nov 16): For nearly four decades, NongShim Co has dominated South Korea’s instant-noodle market with its signature Shin Ramyun. But when Korean ramen became a global phenomenon, it was a rival that captured the world’s appetite — and investors’ imagination.

Samyang Foods Co did it with its Buldak, which became a viral sensation with global fans filming themselves eating the intensely spicy noodles on social media. The craze pushed Samyang’s overseas sales above 80% of revenue — compared with NongShim’s 37% — and lifted its market value to nearly four times that of its rival.

Now NongShim is spending heavily to rebuild investor confidence.

At the heart of the push is a 200 billion won factory for NongShim’s iconic Shin Ramyun in the port city of Busan, the company’s first dedicated export plant and home to what the company calls the world’s fastest instant-noodle production lines. The facility will boost NongShim’s domestic export capacity by 70% as it seeks to regain ground lost to Samyang overseas.

“We may have been somewhat slow in responding to global demand early on because our products were so deeply loved at home for so long,” said Songha Ji, NongShim’s head of global marketing.

A decades-old domestic rivalry between two of South Korea’s biggest food makers is intensifying overseas. NongShim and Samyang, both based in Seoul, are racing to capitalise on a K-food boom that has pushed Korean noodles into mainstream supermarkets from the US to Europe, just as the global instant-noodle market is projected to grow about 23% to US$63.3 billion by 2030.

See also: Coca-Cola raises guidance, buoyed by soda sales abroad

NongShim’s new six-story complex, which opened in October, is designed to produce 600 packets a minute on each line — twice the speed of conventional setups. Inside, raw dough takes barely seven minutes to become a shelf-ready packet of Shin Ramyun. Guided by artificial intelligence sensors and automated mixers, the noodles are rolled, flash-fried and boxed at blinding speed.

The factory will nearly double NongShim’s annual domestic export capacity to 1.2 billion packets and raise its total global capacity to 6.2 billion across Korea and four factories in the US and China. Production from Busan will initially be directed to Japan, Europe, Australia, India and Southeast Asia.

NongShim aims to double global noodle sales to 5.4 trillion won by 2030, which would lift overseas sales to more than 60% of revenue. Such growth would also elevate it to the global top five instant noodle makers alongside Nissin Foods Holdings Co and Maggi-maker Nestlé SA.

See also: Starbucks says it’s not buying Chipotle, dousing deal rumours

NongShim’s push puts it head-to-head with Samyang. The Buldak maker is rapidly gaining ground in overseas markets where NongShim dominated, having already overtaken it in key markets like China and Europe. It is on track to become the third-largest instant noodle seller in the US this year — right behind NongShim, according to Euromonitor International.

Samyang is also accelerating its global expansion and announced last week it would invest more than 131 billion won in a new Vietnamese production line. Its first overseas plant in China is set to open in January.

For NongShim, the test will be whether the new capacity translates into faster sales growth and improved profitability. The company’s valuation could get a lift from a rebound in US sales and increased output from the Busan facility, according to Hanwha Investment & Securities analyst Han Yujung.

NongShim’s push for overseas growth has a promising early start — sales of Shin Ramyun abroad jumped 36% in the first half of this year.

Still, Samyang commands a valuation premium over NongShim, its stock is trading at 13.4 times forward earnings versus the latter’s 11.4 — meaning investors are paying more per won of projected profit in anticipation of faster growth.

NongShim is also borrowing from its rival’s playbook. To court Gen Z shoppers abroad, it has leaned into pop culture — launching limited-edition Shin Ramyun tied to Netflix’s K-Pop Demon Hunters, partnering with K-pop group aespa as global ambassadors and setting up booths at fan conventions globally.

On Monday, Nongshim unveiled a limited seafood edition of Shin Ramyun, co-developed with celebrity chef Edward Lee, to mark the 40th anniversary of the flagship noodle brand. It also plans to roll out a new stir-fried Shin Ramyun next year, entering the soupless-noodle category that propelled Buldak’s global success.

“We cannot yet claim that we are outperforming Samyang in many international markets,” Ji, NongShim’s marketing head, said. “But we are studying and benchmarking what Samyang has done well.”

title: European gas dips as record US flows counter storage concerns
article:
(Nov 16): European natural gas slid as traders weighed milder weather and record exports from the US against persistent worries about the continent’s thin winter inventories.

Benchmark futures fell as much as 4.7% early on Monday before paring some of the losses. Milder weather is set to spread across Europe in the coming days — potentially limiting heating demand — while more supply is coming to the tight global market from the US after projects there increased production to a fresh peak.

The global gas market remains finely balanced, with improving supply prospects offset by winter demand and fierce competition among buyers. Europe’s gas-storage sites are less than 71% full after recent cold spells lifted fuel use, well below the five-year seasonal average of 89%.

“The market is very much tied to volatility as winter demand bites while the supply side looks to improve,” said Florence Schmit, a senior energy strategist at Rabobank.

Over the weekend, Iran targeted a US helicopter base in Bahrain, even as it reiterated that a path to ending the conflict remains open. Attacks on vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz have also continued. Gas prices in Europe are likely to remain elevated so long as the conflict remains unresolved.

See also: Goldman Sachs predicts ‘sizeable surplus’ for oil market in 2027

“The winter balance remains sensitive to weather, supply disruptions and further shifts in market sentiment,” analysts at Timera Energy said in a note.

Dutch front-month futures, Europe’s gas benchmark, traded 1.7% lower at €89.44 a megawatt-hour by 9.07am in Amsterdam. They added more than 6% last week.

title: US diesel falls below US$6 a gallon, easing key inflationary pressure
article:
(Nov 16): US retail diesel prices dropped below US$6 a gallon for the first time since early September, taking some pressure off a key inflationary input that has pushed the price of energy and food higher this fall.

Retail diesel prices dropped to US$5.9989 a gallon on Monday (Nov 16), according to AAA, down from a peak over US$6.50 a gallon in late September.

Diesel supplies have been squeezed tighter than most other fuels since the US-Iran war began, choking off energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz for months. And while crude oil cargoes have recovered, fuel remains curtailed. That shortage has since been exacerbated by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, pushing the country — in normal times the world’s second-largest exporter of diesel — to curb diesel shipments through the end of January.

The resulting price spike has squeezed farmers, truck drivers and everyday consumers in the US and around the world. Diesel is often referred to as the “workhorse fuel of the global economy” for its role in powering tractor-trailers hauling food to grocery stores, farm equipment, home heating and even backup electricity generators at data centres. The economy-wide impacts of higher diesel prices can be seen in wholesale inflation that’s risen at the fastest pace since 2022.

The White House worked to rein in diesel costs ahead of this fall’s midterm elections, with a range of measures from loosening restrictions around a tax-free dyed variant of the fuel to attempting to import diesel from Russia. The efforts, at least electorally, proved largely unsuccessful, with Republicans suffering historic losses.

To be sure, prices have come down meaningfully and fleet-wide supply agreements often allow truckers to pay less for fuel than the listed retail price. Meanwhile, heating oil futures settled Friday near US$4.26 a gallon — well off the highest prices this year.

See also: European gas dips as record US flows counter storage concerns

But that’s the highest seasonal price ever recorded. The retail price, similarly, is still above the highest price ever recorded before 2026.

title: Burnham set to say Brexit has not worked
article:
(Nov 16): UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will tell an audience in London’s financial district on Monday that Brexit has not worked and a new deal must be sought, starting at a summit with the European Union (EU) later this week.

The prime minister will follow convention by giving a speech about foreign policy at the Lord Mayor’s banquet. He will argue that the world has changed since the EU referendum of 2016, meaning that the UK should have a closer relationship with its neighbouring democracies.

“The Brexit we were given has not worked,” Burnham is expected to say, according to pre-briefed remarks. “We have lost more than we gained.”

The speech kicks off a crucial week for two of the government’s most politically sensitive policies. On Tuesday, Alan Milburn — a former Labour minister who served under Tony Blair — will publish a report on Britain’s youth unemployment crisis. Burnham’s government has pledged to get more young people into work and eventually reduce the country’s huge welfare costs.

“Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” the Labour leader wrote in an opinion article in the Guardian newspaper on Sunday.

Also over the weekend, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said young people who have been unemployed for a year would be guaranteed work under an expanded government programme. Ministers are expected to reveal more details of Labour’s plan to boost job opportunities following publication of Milburn’s report.

See also: UK's Burnham tries to hush down his own talk of rejoining EU

Then, on Friday, UK officials arrive in Brussels for a delayed summit with the EU. Burnham is pursuing a new deal that targets a modest number of areas including trade barriers on agrifood products, a youth mobility programme and linking of emissions trading systems.

Speaking to broadcasters ahead of the speech on Monday morning, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the Brexit deal had hurt trade with the EU, and Burnham is seeking to fix that.

People voted for Brexit “primarily because they wanted positive economic change”, Miliband said on Sky News. “Unfortunately we have had the opposite.”

See also: Asda’s flat sales end losing streak as new CEO joins UK grocer

In his speech at the Lord Mayor’s banquet, Burnham is expected to acknowledge that some sectors have adapted to Brexit — a possible nod to the financial sector. However, he will argue that businesses as a whole are worse off, as are consumers.

The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), a lobby group, urged Burnham to come back with a deal that reduces the cost of trade, adding that the current arrangements — sealed by former prime minister Boris Johnson — are “still failing to deliver, almost six years after Brexit”.

In a statement on Sunday night, the BCC said “businesses face customs, VAT (value-added tax), regulatory and mobility barriers, alongside rising protectionism, global subsidies and the EU’s emerging ‘Made in Europe’ agenda”. Over half of exporters want EU customs paperwork and delays at the border to be removed, a BCC survey showed.

title: Malaysian data centre loan syndication delayed in rare deal pause
article:
(Nov 16): A US$488 million ($628.8 million) loan for a Malaysian data centre project backed by private equity firm Actis has been delayed while being marketed to other lenders, according to people familiar with the matter.

A planned online presentation scheduled for Nov 2 by loan arrangers for other banks invited to participate in the financing by Epoch Digital Pte Ltd didn’t take place, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information. A visit planned for the same week to the data centre, whose computing capacity will be used by TikTok owner ByteDance Ltd, also failed to happen.

Lead arrangers HSBC Holdings Plc, Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp and Bank of China have signed the loan and committed to providing Epoch Digital with the funds, according to the people. But the missed online presentation and site visit are important and standard steps for prospective banks that need to undertake due diligence on the loan before deciding to participate in syndication, and mark a rare postponement.

Management of Epoch Digital wasn’t available on the scheduled dates, prompting the delay in the syndication timeline, said one of the people.

A representative for London-based Actis declined to comment, while Epoch Digital didn’t respond to a request for comment. Spokespeople for HSBC and SMBC declined to comment, while representatives from AIIB and Bank of China didn’t immediately respond.

The delay points to the complexities around financing the AI buildout as a growing number of new players rush to meet the demand for computing capacity, while lenders juggle the flood of borrowing requests against internal exposure limits. PricewaterhouseCoopers estimates spending on data centres could reach US$8.2 trillion in the Asia-Pacific by 2050, though the facilities globally face growing pushback from citizens concerned about their societal impact.

See also: Nvidia’s CEO search draws fire with Bessent’s ‘shake-up’ call

The online presentation and site visit are being coordinated for new dates, said the people.

Owned almost totally by Actis-managed funds, Epoch Digital was established in November 2022 and its first data centre development was in Taiwan, details on Actis’ website show.

Arrangers had reserved the right to amend the syndication timetable at any time, according to the people. Banks syndicating loans in Asia typically like to keep deals moving smoothly along timetables laid out in invitations to other lenders.

title: US, partners agree to safeguard key AI tech, infrastructure
article:
(Nov 16): The US and nine partner nations including India, Singapore and the UK signed a pledge to safeguard sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure amid escalating strategic competition with China over the future of artificial intelligence (AI).

The “San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity” establishes a framework for the protection of critical goods, software, knowledge materials, and components essential to AI supply chains.

The pact targets those items “whose theft, illicit transfer, or acquisition by hostile actors would confer a meaningful military or intelligence advantage”, the US State Department said in a statement.

The joint actions comes amid an urgent reassessment in Washington over how to control the exports and use of top-tier accelerators by China. The debate has been sparked by revelations that Nvidia Corp’s chief Jensen Huang had an affair with a former data centre executive whom the US suspects is a Chinese spy.

It also comes days before US President Donald Trump is expected to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

Part of the broader US-led “Pax Silica” initiative, the agreement also covers vital physical and digital infrastructure including ports, transport systems, communications and logistics networks, “whose disruption, degradation, hostile control, or the unauthorised exposure of the data flowing through them would cause significant harm or dysfunction”.

See also: Post-Jensen US chip curbs threaten Southeast Asia’s AI boom

The declaration underscores Washington’s broader push to institutionalise allied economic security architecture as competition with China over frontier technologies intensifies. The other signatories are Australia, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

Asked about the development during a regular press briefing on Monday, China Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning said “we should not draw ideological lines or form exclusive cliques” when it comes to AI. “Parties should join hands in promoting development and governance of AI and make it serve the common well-being of humanity”.

Asked if Xi and Trump would discuss they issue when they meet later this week, she said “both sides are in communication in this regard”.

See also: Why compute will be the next big AI trade

South Korea’s Second Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Kim Jina attended a Pax Silica retreat hosted by the US Department of State in San Francisco on Sunday and signed the agreement, the Foreign Ministry said on Monday. Kim discussed ways for “like-minded nations to cooperate in building a trustworthy AI ecosystem”.

Japan’s Foreign Ministry also confirmed that the government signed the economic-security focused declaration on Sunday with like-minded nations, as part of initiatives under Pax Silica.

The US State Department said participating governments plan to establish joint working groups covering pro-innovation policy frameworks, AI adoption in key sectors, supply chain cooperation, safe harbours and supply chain security hubs, and AI security and resilience.

They also pledged coordinated efforts to address economic coercion and supply chain disruptions, while seeking to protect private investment and ensure “a level playing field for innovation and growth”.

Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden are also expected to sign the declaration in the coming days, according to the Financial Times, which reported the agreement earlier.

title: China’s economy disappoints with stimulus yet to lift investment
article:
(Nov 16): China’s growth weakened across the board in October as investment unexpectedly worsened while consumption and industrial output undershot estimates, in a sign Beijing’s latest stimulus measures have yet to feed through to the economy.

Retail sales rose just 0.4% from a year ago, a sharp slowdown from September and far below the consensus forecast of 0.8% by economists polled by Bloomberg. Industrial output expanded at a slower rate for the first time in three months and grew 4.8% in October.

Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in the first 10 months of 2026 from the same period last year, lower than the 7% decline expected by economists. For the single month of October, investment contracted 17% from 2025, according to Bloomberg Economics, its sharpest fall outside the Covid-19 pandemic.

“We are still in the waiting period for the stimulus impact to kick in,” said Helen Qiao, the chief economist for Greater China at BofA Global Research. Policymakers “are probably expecting things to get worse from here in 2027 and 2028, and there’s a willingness to hold back some of the stimulus,” she told Bloomberg TV.

The figures revealed an economy that’s again at risk of losing momentum, even after Beijing stepped up efforts to bolster growth in late September. What especially stood out was the sharp deterioration in investment, a key lever long used by officials to stimulate growth during downturns.

See also: China car output slows to four-year low as domestic demand drops

Economists had expected the investment decline to narrow, after the government rolled out greater public borrowing quota and accelerated spending on major construction projects via a 800 billion-yuan (US$120 billion or $154 billion) programme. That makes a deepening fall in capital expenditure on infrastructure all the more perplexing.

There’s a rising concern that a confluence of political and economic factors is crippling the once-powerful tool.

An ongoing leadership reshuffle of the Communist Party — which will culminate in a major congress next year — could make cadres more cautious about committing to projects, a sentiment likely fanned by the raging anti-corruption campaign.

See also: Due diligence for China directors

In addition, a mid-2027 deadline to eliminate local government financing vehicles — platforms that carried “hidden” or off-balance-sheet debt amassed by authorities in the provinces — likely also distracted officials from new projects as they scrambled to clean up the old borrowing.

Any major economic reforms will likely be deferred until after the Communist Party holds its 2027 congress and ushers in the next generation of decision makers, according to Carlos Casanova, a senior economist for Asia at Union Bancaire Privee.

Coupled with the anti-corruption campaign, “this could contribute to policy paralysis and weigh on economic growth in the fourth quarter of 2026 and 2027”, he said.

In a sign Beijing has ample fiscal dry powder, government deposits at banks in October increased substantially more than what normal seasonal patterns would imply, suggesting the funds raised in the fourth quarter may only be used in early 2027 to support growth, according to Goldman Sachs Group Inc economists. Public spending fell for the seventh straight month in September.

Other details in Monday’s report point to the widening divergence in the economy. While electronics manufacturing output surged nearly 20% in October from a year ago thanks to the global boom in artificial intelligence investment, car production slowed sharply and climbed just 0.9%, the worst reading since the end of Covid. Intense competition and falling sales mean carmakers are headed for another year of record low profit margins.

As domestic demand weakens, retail sales are on track to finish the year with the weakest growth since the pandemic. Their performance isn’t much different even if cars are excluded.

Residential prices continued to fall in October, extending a slump that’s dragged on economic growth for more than five years. Property investment plunged 21.6% in the first 10 months of the year from a year earlier, compared with a 20.6% decline in January-September.

The statistics agency described the state of the economy as “overall stable” and said it had “extended a trend of renewing growth engines and improving its structure”, In a statement, the National Bureau of Statistics highlighted challenges faced by the economy include an uncertain global environment, imbalances between supply and demand, as well as difficulties in some businesses’ operations.

Despite indications that growth has come under pressure, the urban surveyed jobless rate unexpectedly slipped to 5.1% last month from 5.2% in September. Many economists see the official unemployment measure as an incomplete reflection of the labour market because it excludes migrant workers who returned to the countryside after losing work.

The economy rebounded in the third quarter, with growth reaching the lower end of Beijing’s annual target of 4.5% to 5%. But the recovery remained heavily reliant on overseas demand, with net exports contributing almost 40% of the increase in gross domestic product (GDP) — the most for any quarter since the start of 2025.

That dependence is becoming a bigger risk as questions mount over the sustainability of the global artificial intelligence investment boom, which has powered demand for Chinese electronics and other manufactured goods. A slowdown in exports would increase pressure on domestic consumption and investment to pick up the slack.

At the same time, after GDP expanded 4.6% in the first three quarters from a year ago, officials can tolerate some slowdown in the final months. The economy only needs to grow 4.3% in the last quarter for China’s full-year GDP to hit the lower bound of the official goal.

The October figures will be closely scrutinised by top officials ahead of the Central Economic Work Conference, usually held in the first half of December. The gathering will offer clues on Beijing’s economic priorities for 2027 and the scale of any additional support.

Policymakers may lean more heavily on fiscal measures if the economy loses further momentum.

The People’s Bank of China has signalled caution about cutting interest rates when borrowing demand is already weak. And in a potential sign of unease over market expectations for further easing, the central bank is draining funds from the financial system via a medium-term liquidity facility for the first time in five months.

“The Chinese authorities need to find out the reason behind the investment cliff,” said Raymond Yeung, the chief economist for Greater China at Australia and New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “This is an area where fiscal policy can play a significant role.”
